sens: To put in hand, deliver to someone
To choose someone for a mission or function
To determine an intention, a design
G4400.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literally to put something in hand, to deliver it: this is the basic image of the Greek word. In Acts 3:20, Jesus is the one whom God has "destined" for us, meaning He has made Him available to us, like a gift delivered into the hands of those who believe.
2. More often, the word means to choose someone for a specific function or mission. In Acts 22:14, God has "destined" Paul to know His will and to see the Just One: He has elected him, set him apart for this particular knowledge. Similarly, in Acts 26:16, the Lord has "appointed" him as a minister and witness, meaning He has decided and determined that he would be His servant to testify.
3. In the background, there is also the idea of a firm intention, a design that one takes and seizes: God determines to do something with someone.
G4400.origine: The Greek word is composed of "pro" (before, in advance) and "chéir" (the hand), with the verbal suffix "izo". The basic image is therefore one of "taking in hand in advance," or "making available." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the same Greek word translates verbs like "send" (שָׁלַח) or "take" (לָקַח), which shows that it expresses the idea of a decided and implemented action.
G4400.emploi: The verb "destine" appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Acts, and always in a context of divine action. Acts 3:20 uses it to designate Jesus as the one whom God has prepared for our salvation. Acts 22:14 and 26:16 use it to express God's choice of Paul for a specific mission: to know Him and to serve Him. It is a word that emphasizes divine sovereignty and the divine plan before and beyond any human will.
G4400.portee: This word reveals that our life and mission are not the result of chance, but of God's design. For the believer, being "destined" by God to know His will or to serve Him means that our life has a divine purpose, inscribed even before our first steps. It is a word of comfort: we are not lost in the universe, but "put in hand" by the One who loves us.

sens: To designate or elect someone before the opportunity arises
To prepare someone in advance for a mission or function
G4401.detail:
1. The verb expresses the idea of making a deliberate choice, but placing it in the past — before the event occurs. In Acts 10:41, Peter speaks of the witnesses that God has "chosen beforehand" to be witnesses of the resurrection of Christ. God did not designate them at the moment Jesus appeared to them; He had destined them for this role even before the resurrection took place.
2. The word thus emphasizes a prior intention and preparation: it is not an improvised or casual choice, but a thoughtful election, determined in advance by the one who chooses. It is a voluntary act that anticipates events.
G4401.origine: The Greek verb is composed of "pro" (before) and "cheirotoneō" (to choose, literally "to raise the hand to vote"). The basic image is that of voting by raising hands in the Athenian Assembly, from which comes the meaning "to choose" or "to elect." By adding "pro" at the beginning, we obtain the idea of an election that precedes the moment of need. The simple verb "cheirotoneō" also appears in the New Testament (Acts 14:23; 2 Corinthians 8:19).
G4401.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament (Acts 10:41). It describes God's divine choice of the witnesses of the resurrection: God had designated them beforehand, even before Jesus rose. This compound form emphasizes the aspect of predestination or pre-ordination — not that God determines our actions, but that He has a pre-formed intention regarding the people He chooses for important roles. The context is Peter's proclamation to the centurion Cornelius.
G4401.portee: This word invites the believer to grasp that God does not choose His witnesses and servants by chance or at the last minute. Those who are called to bear witness to the Gospel, those who are chosen for a mission, have been chosen with intention and anticipation by God. This provides profound assurance: our calling is not accidental; it responds to a predetermined plan.

sens: Deacon of the Church of Jerusalem during the time of the apostles
G4402.detail: Prochore is one of the seven men chosen by the assembly of disciples to serve at tables and distribute aid to widows in the early Church (Acts 6:5). His name literally means "the one who leads the choir" in Greek, but in this biblical context, he is known as one of the first deacons, men full of faith and the Holy Spirit, entrusted with a practical and sacred mission in service to the community.
G4402.origine: The name Prochore comes from ancient Greek: "pro" means "before" or "in front," and "choros" means "choir" or "dance"—literally "the one who leads the choir." It is a common Greek name among the early Jewish Christians who spoke Greek in Jerusalem. In later ecclesiastical history, Prochore is associated with the apostle John, of whom he is said to have been a companion and secretary according to tradition.
G4402.emploi: Prochore appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:5, where he is listed among the seven elected deacons. This event takes place in the very early days of the Church, after Pentecost, when the apostles asked the assembly to choose men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, to manage material aid and allow the apostles to devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the Word. Prochore, Philip, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicholas, a proselyte from Antioch, with Stephen as the first mentioned, embody this new diaconal service in the young Church.
G4402.portee: The ministry of Prochore reminds us that humble and practical service—distributing food, caring for widows—is a sacred calling in the Church, no less important than preaching. His inclusion among the first deacons shows that authentic faith is manifested in concrete attention to the needs of others and in the love that moves hands as much as the heart.

sens: The rear part of a ship, the part that follows the movement of the hull in the water
The area towards the back, by topographical extension
G4403.detail:
1. The stern is the rear part of a boat, the end that is behind when sailing: it is the opposite of the bow (the front). In Mark 4:38, Jesus is sleeping at the stern on a cushion during the crossing of the Sea of Galilee. In Acts 27:29 and 27:41, it is from the stern that the anchors are thrown and the ship is broken against the rocks: it is the most exposed part to shocks and waves when the ship runs aground.
2. By extension, "stern" simply refers to the rear area of anything that moves forward, whether a ship or another floating structure, without figurative connotation.
G4403.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek adjective meaning "rear" or "posterior." It is formed from a root that expresses the idea of "behind," "in the back." It is a technical term from ancient navigation, whose family is found in other Mediterranean languages.
G4403.emploi: The word appears only three times in Greek in the New Testament, all in nautical contexts. In Mark 4:38, it locates the place where Jesus sleeps during the storm. In Acts 27:29-41, it appears twice in the detailed account of Paul's shipwreck: first when the anchors are thrown "from the stern" to stabilize the approaching ship, and then when the stern "is broken by the violence of the waves" while the bow remains stuck. The term is purely descriptive and technical.
G4403.portee: Although technical, this word helps us to concretely visualize the biblical scenes: where Jesus slept, how the sailors tried to save Paul's ship. These details make the narrative vivid and verifiable, anchoring the Word in a precise geography and reality.

sens: The first part of the day, from sunrise or dawn until around noon
The moment when one gets up and daily activities begin
Dawn, the hour before sunrise
The instant of sunrise itself
Figuratively: the beginning, the start of a period
G4404.detail:
1. Morning is the first part of the day, the one that follows the night and precedes noon. It is the natural moment when light returns. In Matthew 21:18, it is "the morning" when Jesus, returning to the city, felt hungry — it designates this early hour of the day that begins.
2. It is also the hour when people get up and start their activities: in Mark 1:35 (implicitly by context), Jesus rises "very early in the morning" to pray, before anyone is awake. Thus, it is the moment of awakening and the beginning of work.
3. The word can refer to dawn, that still dark moment before sunrise. John 20:1 specifies: "early in the morning, while it was still dark," Mary Magdalene came to the tomb — this is before the day is truly risen.
4. Sometimes it simply describes the moment of sunrise: in Mark 16:2, the women come to the tomb "in the morning, at sunrise."
5. Exceptionally, in Matthew 16:3, "storm" also translates this word: there is a fixed meteorological expression, "stormy sky in the morning" (as we say today "red sky in the morning"), where the word retains its temporal meaning but is used in a proverbial formula.
G4404.origine: The word comes from the preposition π ρό (before), figuratively: morning is the time that comes before the rest of the day. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it generally translates בֹּקֶר (boker), which literally means the moment when night breaks — a very ancient root in Semitic languages. The Greek πρωΐ emphasizes the temporal aspect: what comes first, what precedes.
G4404.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and John). It situates important moments in the Gospel narrative. Jesus rises "in the morning" to pray (Mark 1:35), he curses the fig tree "in the morning" and returns "in the morning" to see the results (Mark 11:20). The women discover the resurrection "in the morning" of the first day of the week (John 20:1, Mark 16:9). The Sanhedrin meets "in the morning" to deliver Jesus to Pilate (Mark 15:1). In Acts 28:23, Paul speaks to the Jews "from morning until evening." The adverb always places the action at the early hour, often to emphasize urgency, diligence, or the solemn beginning of an event.
G4404.portee: For the Christian reader, morning is the time when God acts and where the disciples act: resurrection at dawn, Jesus' morning prayer, the diligence of the women who hurry to the tomb. It is the hour of renewal and meeting with the Lord. This invites the believer to see morning as a privileged time for prayer and waiting on God.

sens: The first part of the day, when the sun rises
The moment of daybreak, dawn
G4405.detail:
1. Morning designates the first part of the day, which begins when the sun rises. In Matthew 27:1, morning arrives and it is the moment when the chief priests and the elders gather to judge Jesus: this shows that morning is a turning point of the day, a pivotal moment when one moves from night to light.
2. More precisely, morning can refer to dawn, that very early moment when the day begins to break. In John 21:4, Jesus is on the shore "when morning had come": the disciples do not recognize him right away, which suggests a still weak light, that of early morning. It is this moment of transition between night and full day.
G4405.origine: The word comes from πρῶι (prôi), which means "early in the morning" or "at dawn." It is an adjective that has taken on a substantive meaning: "the moment of morning." In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates this word as בֹּקֶר (boker), which also means dawn or morning, that moment when God renews his creation and brings light.
G4405.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, always in Matthew and John. In both cases, it marks a decisive moment: in Matthew, it is the morning of Christ's passion, when the Sanhedrin gathers to condemn him to death; in John, it is the morning of the resurrection, when Jesus appears alive to his disciples. Morning is thus the moment when crucial events of salvation unfold and resolve.
G4405.portee: Morning, in the biblical narrative, is never neutral: it is the hour of judgment and revelation. In Matthew, it introduces the condemnation of Jesus to death; in John, it announces his resurrection and victory. For the Christian reader, morning reminds us that God acts in history, that dawn always follows night, and that it is often when everything seems lost that God intervenes.

sens: Rain that falls at the beginning of the agricultural season, after sowing
What comes first, arriving early in the natural cycle
Figuratively: grace or blessing that first manifests in the believer's life
G4406.detail:
1. The word literally designates the early rain or "first season rain" that falls after sowing in the autumn in the Promised Land. This rain was essential for the germination of grains. In James 5:7, Paul encourages believers to have the patience of the farmer who waits for this rain: "Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until he receives the early and late rains."
2. By extension, the term expresses the idea of what comes first, at the beginning of a cycle or period. The structure of the word refers to the beginning, the starting point in time.
3. In a spiritual reading, it evokes the blessings that God first grants to the believer who waits with confidence, just as the farmer receives the rain that precedes the harvest.
G4406.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "before" or "early," close to "proto-" (first). It is closely related to πρώιος (prôios), which also means "early" or "of the morning." In Hebrew, this term translates יוֹרֶה (yoreh), which specifically designates the autumn rain in the Promised Land — the early rain essential for crops. The Greek of the Septuagint has preserved this concrete image of the Palestinian climate.
G4406.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 5:7. It is used in a context of exhortation to patience: the believer must wait for the coming of the Lord with the same patient confidence as the farmer who knows that the early rain will come to fertilize his field. This unique usage reflects the agricultural background of the Middle East, where the early rain was a vital necessity and a sign of divine providence. The image is rich: just as the farmer cannot force the rain but must wait for it, the believer cannot force the return of Christ but must receive it with humble trust and active patience.
G4406.portee: This word invites the believer to cultivate patient hope. Just as the farmer understands the laws of nature and accepts the time they require, the Christian is called to recognize God's timing and trust in his providence. The early rain symbolizes the first graces received: it nourishes faith and prepares it for the final harvest that will come at Christ's return.

sens: Belonging to the morning, the early hours of the day
(Figuratively) Shining with the brightness of the dawn, heralding light
G4407.detail:
1. The word simply describes what relates to the morning, to dawn or the early hours of the day — the moment when the sun rises. In Revelation, "the morning star" (Revelation 2:28; 22:16) refers to the celestial body that shines in the sky just before sunrise, the brightest of all stars at that moment of the night.
2. Figuratively, this morning star becomes an image of the coming of Christ, of His glory and the promise of salvation that He brings. It evokes the light that dispels darkness, hope, and final victory. The expression "the bright morning star" in Revelation 22:16 identifies Jesus Himself as this light that heralds the renewal of all things.
G4407.origine: The word comes from πρωί (prôi), which means "early, in the morning." It is a classical adjective used to qualify what is "of the morning" or "morning-related." In the Old Testament, this word generally translates the Hebrew בֹּקֶר (boqer), the ordinary word for "morning." This image of the morning star was already known in ancient literature as a symbol of hope and new dawn.
G4407.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Revelation in relation to the same image: the morning star. In Revelation 2:28, Jesus promises the victor "the morning star" as a reward. In Revelation 22:16, the resurrected and glorified Christ directly identifies Himself with this "bright morning star." This recurring image emphasizes that morning represents for John the moment of Christ's final triumph, the eternal dawn that follows the night of the present world.
G4407.portee: For the believer, this designation of Christ as "the morning star" speaks of His glorious return and the definitive light He will bring. It invites one to see beyond the current darkness and to await with confidence the manifestation of His glory. It is a call to perseverance and hope in the one who comes to renew all things.

sens: The front part of a ship, the part that cuts through the water first
By extension, the front of a boat in general and its equipment
G4408.detail:
1. The bow is the front part of a ship, the part that is at the front and moves first to cut through the waves. It is the pointed end of the boat opposite the stern (the back). In the account of Paul's shipwreck in Malta (Acts 27), this distinction is clearly seen: the ship runs aground in two parts, the bow remains stuck in the sandbank while the stern breaks apart under the violence of the waves (Acts 27:41).
2. The word is also used to refer to the equipment of the bow, particularly the anchors that were attached there. When the sailors attempt to escape from the doomed ship, they pretend to "drop the anchors from the bow" (Acts 27:30), meaning to let the anchors attached to the bow slide to stabilize the boat.
G4408.origine: The Greek word "prōra" simply designates the bow of the ship. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of moving forward, going ahead. It is a technical term of maritime vocabulary, rarely used in biblical texts, appearing only in Luke's account in Acts to describe the ship from Alexandria that was carrying Paul to Rome.
G4408.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both passages in the account of Paul's journey in Acts 27. It is very specialized, technical, and maritime vocabulary. Luke uses it to specify the details of the shipwreck: first in Acts 27:30 to mention the anchors of the bow that the sailors pretend to lower, and then in Acts 27:41 to describe how the bow of the ship sank into the sandbank while the stern was breaking apart. It is a term that only a narrator attentive to nautical details would use.
G4408.portee: This word reminds us that the Gospel connects with the concrete and technical realities of life. By recounting Paul's shipwreck with authentic maritime vocabulary, Luke lends credibility to his account and shows that God was present even in the details of a terrifying storm at sea. It is a small example of Luke's faithfulness to the truth of the facts.

sens: to occupy the first place, to be at the forefront
to have preeminence, superiority
to dominate, to command
G4409.detail:
1. To be first means to occupy the first place, to be at the forefront, ahead of all others. The word evokes the image of a procession or ranking where one is placed in front: it is to be first among all.
2. To have preeminence means to possess recognized superiority, to be above others in importance, power, or dignity. In Colossians 1:18, Paul states that Christ "is to be first in everything": this means that Jesus has a place of honor and absolute dominion over all things.
3. To dominate or command is the natural consequence of this first place: the one who is first has authority and governance.
G4409.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "prôtos" which means "first" — the root expresses order or rank. Adding the suffix "-euô" transforms the adjective into a verb: "to be first" becomes "to exercise the quality of being first." This family of words is found in "protos" (first), "protostatos" (one who stands in the first rank), and many other compounds where "proto-" marks the beginning or primacy.
G4409.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 1:18. Paul uses it to express that Christ is preeminent in everything — it is a rare and solemn word, chosen to give full force to the affirmation of Jesus' universal lordship. The context shows that this preeminence concerns His role as head of the Church and His resurrection from the dead: He is the firstborn who dominates and governs the entire body.
G4409.portee: This word reveals the fundamental conviction of the New Testament: Jesus Christ is not just an important figure, He is first in all things. For the Christian, recognizing that Jesus "is first" means accepting His complete lordship, giving Him the first place in one's life, thoughts, and choices. It is a call to total allegiance to the one who governs the universe and the Church.

sens: Seat of honor in a synagogue or a banquet, placed in the most prominent position
Visible mark of prestige and social rank
Human desire for distinction and public recognition
G4410.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the seat reserved for honor in places of worship or meals. In a synagogue, it was a place of honor facing the assembly; at a table, the most prestigious seat. Jesus cites this example when He reproaches the Pharisees and scribes for loving "the first seats in the synagogues" (Matthew 23:6).
2. This practice reveals the deep desire to be distinguished and socially recognized. The "first seats" symbolize the quest for prestige: those who seek them want everyone to see and honor them. Luke 11:43 shows that the Pharisees "love the first seats" while also loving "greetings in the marketplaces."
3. In a spiritual sense, this term illustrates the danger of cultivating religious pride: seeking the honor of men rather than the glory of God. The scribes who "seek the first seats" (Mark 12:39) illustrate how the desire for prestige can corrupt piety.
G4410.origine: The Greek word combines "prôtos" (first, highest in rank) and "kathedra" (seat, chair). It literally describes the most important place, that of the master or notable. The term is coined to name this very specific social reality: the seat that marks the status of the one who sits there.
G4410.emploi: The word appears only four times in Greek, always in the Synoptic Gospels. Jesus uses it each time to criticize the religious leaders of His time: Pharisees and scribes who visibly seek this prestige. It is not just a matter of comfort, but of vanity. The context reveals a progression: first the criticism of their love for "the first seats" (Matthew 23:6, Mark 12:39, Luke 20:46), then the explicit warning against this covetousness as a sign of a heart far from God (Luke 11:43).
G4410.portee: This word challenges every believer tempted to cultivate their image or status in the Church. Jesus warns us: seeking the first place is to forget that the kingdom of God reverses the values of the world. True honor comes not from the recognition of men, but from faithfulness to God and service to others.

sens: the most honored position at a meal
the most prominent seat in a religious assembly
the situation of one who occupies the highest rank
G4411.detail:
1. At a table, during a feast or banquet, the first place was the head of the table, reserved for the main host or the person of greatest prestige. This is exactly what Jesus criticizes about the Pharisees in Matthew 23:6: "they love the first place at feasts," showing how they ostentatiously sought this position of honor.
2. In synagogues, the first place referred to the most visible and prestigious seats where important figures — the scribes and Pharisees — would sit. Mark 12:39 depicts them as "seeking the first seats in the synagogues," revealing their pride.
3. Figuratively, it is the position of superiority and social prestige. Luke 14:7-8 recounts Jesus' parable: a guest who chooses the first place risks being humiliated if someone more important arrives — the image of the seat becomes that of rank and honor.
G4411.origine: The Greek word πρωτοκλισία (prōtoklisia) is composed of "prôtos" (first, principal) and "klisis" (seating position, arrangement at the table). It literally evokes the "first lodging" or the "first position at the banquet." It is a very specialized word, coined to precisely designate this custom of ancient meals.
G4411.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, only in the first three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke), never in John or the rest of the New Testament. Each occurrence is in a context of criticism of religious or social pride. Matthew 23:6 and Mark 12:39 mention it together to show that the scribes and Pharisees seek these honors at the very heart of synagogues and meals. Luke uses it more: in 14:7-8, Jesus teaches by parable that one should not take the first place for oneself, out of humility; in 20:46, He warns His disciples to beware of the scribes who covet these seats. The word always designates a real position (at the table or in the synagogue) that embodies a spiritual value: the love of earthly glory and human recognition.
G4411.portee: This term reveals Jesus' view on pride and humility. For Him, seeking the first places — whether social, religious, or honorary — reflects a heart turned away from God. In contrast, the Kingdom of God values the one who allows themselves to be placed, who claims nothing, who accepts the last place. This word calls the believer to examine their heart: do they seek recognition, prestige, the first place? Or are they free from these desires, turning their gaze toward Jesus rather than their own glory?

sens: Who comes before others in the order of time or succession.
Who occupies the highest rank, the most important.
In the first place, first (adverb).
Who is past, anterior.
G4413G.detail:
1. First in temporal or spatial succession: it is the one who arrives before all others, who leads the way. Jesus tells His disciple: "First go and be reconciled to your brother" (Matthew 5:24), showing that reconciliation must precede the offering. John ran faster and arrived first at the tomb (John 20:4). This simply designates chronological or positional order.

2. First in rank, importance, dignity: the one of the highest quality or status. Jesus tells His disciples: "If anyone wants to be first, he must be last of all and servant of all" (Mark 9:35), showing that true primacy comes through humility and service.

3. As an adverb, "firstly" or "first": indicates the order in which things should be done or the priority to be given. "Clean the inside of the cup first" (Matthew 23:26): the inside must be purified before the outside, which is logically and morally first.

4. Anterior, past: what has occurred before, the condition or state of before. A demon cast out returns with others more wicked, and "the last condition of that man is worse than the first" (Luke 11:26), meaning that the original state was better.
G4413G.origine: The Greek word πρῶτος comes from an Indo-European root meaning "in front," "before." It is the superlative of πρό (before, in front). The primary image is that of what projects forward, which is at the head. In the translation of the Hebrew text of the Old Testament into Greek, it renders the word ראשון (richone, first, chief) and sometimes אחד (one), emphasizing the idea of what is initial or principal. The family of words "pro" in French (prochain, profil, proposer) echoes this distant root.
G4413G.emploi: The word πρῶτος appears 135 times in the New Testament, notably in all the Gospels and the epistles. It designates either a simple chronological or spatial order (John arrives first at the tomb), or a hierarchical rank or moral value (the first in the Kingdom is the last). The Gospel traverses it with a characteristic tension: the social order of the world places the first in front, but Jesus reverses this scheme — "many who are first will be last" (Matthew 19:30, Mark 10:31). Paul uses it to mark priorities: "I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins" (1 Corinthians 15:3), emphasizing what is fundamental. The word thus takes on an ethical, theological hue: what is first in the eyes of God is not first in the eyes of the world.
G4413G.portee: This word teaches a profound spiritual lesson: being first according to God requires serving (Mark 9:35), reconciling before offering, seeing first the plank in one's own eye. It invites the believer to rethink the order of priorities. In a world where everyone aspires to be first, Jesus proposes a reversal: true greatness consists in being last. Meditating on πρῶτος is to ask oneself: what is truly first in my life? Faith, justice, service, or my personal interest?

sens: That which comes first in time or order
That which occupies the first rank, the most important
That which has preceded, that which was before
That which comes before all others in a list or succession
G4413H.detail:
1. First in time or order: the word designates what happens or is placed before everything else. When John the Baptist says that Jesus "preceded me," he means that Jesus, who came after him historically, surpassed him in importance and dignity (John 1:15). This is also the meaning of "before": "he hated me before you" means that before hating you, the world first hated me (John 15:18).

2. The most important, the principal: in a hierarchy or enumeration, that which occupies the first place of dignity or power. This can qualify a city as "first" (capital or metropolis), or in a list of commandments, the one that comes first.

3. That which occurred beforehand, previously: the word can also mean "before that," marking a temporal precedence. When Nicodemus went "beforehand" to Jesus, it describes a visit prior to the one that the Gospel now reports (John 19:39).

4. Used as an adverb or particle: "also," "furthermore," marking the sequence or addition in a narrative. Here the word emphasizes that there are other elements to consider, as in "he also descended" (Ephesians 4:9).
G4413H.origine: The word comes from the Greek root that expresses the idea of "in front," "ahead." It is formed as a superlative: "the most first," meaning that which surpasses all others in precedence. In Hebrew, it primarily translates "rishon" (ראשוֹן), which literally means "that which is at the head," "that which begins." This image of "head" or "beginning" unites the two languages: what is first is that which leads or from which everything proceeds.
G4413H.emploi: The word appears very frequently in the New Testament to situate events in time (the first day of the Sabbath, the first prison), to mark rank and dignity (the first commandment, the first apostle), or to express logical and temporal precedence. In John, it takes on a particular richness: John the Baptist uses it to express that Jesus, although he came after him in history, absolutely surpasses him in dignity and essence — he was "before" (John 1:15, 1:30). The word can also denote a narrative succession, that which comes first in a narrative or enumeration. This versatility — temporal, ordinal, hierarchical — makes it a fundamental word for ordering and classifying everything that the Bible recounts.
G4413H.portee: Understanding the biblical "first" invites reflection on what truly matters: is it the chronological order, or dignity and essence? John the Baptist teaches us that Jesus, although he came after him in time, was "first" as Lord and God. This reminds Christians that true hierarchies do not always follow the appearances of the world, and that the Lord can completely overturn the order that one believes is established.

sens: That which comes before others in time or space
That which occupies the first rank, which has the greatest importance or dignity
First, in the first place (adverb)
G4413I.detail:
1. That which occurs or is situated before other things: in a temporal or spatial succession, the first element. For example, in a meal or a meeting, the chief characters are those who present themselves or intervene before others.
2. That which has the most importance, authority, or dignity in a group or community. It is the one who leads, who matters. In Acts 13:50, the "chief men of the city" are the influential notables who have weight to persecute Paul. In Acts 28:7, Publius is the "chief man of the island," the one who owns the largest lands and receives guests. In Acts 28:17, Paul summons the "chief of the Jews," the leaders of the community. In Mark 6:21, the "chiefs" of Galilee are the high dignitaries invited to the king's feast.
3. When functioning as an adverb ("first"), it indicates the order or logical priority of an enumeration. In Romans 3:2, Paul states that the advantage of the Jews is great "first of all" because God entrusted them with his oracles — this is the first of the advantages to enumerate.
G4413I.origine: The Greek word πρῶτος comes from an Indo-European root related to the idea of "going forward" and "being first." In Hebrew, it is the common translation of רִאשׁוֹן (rišôn, "first"), which also designates that which is at the head. In biblical Greek, πρῶτος can mean both the first in a succession and the first in rank, the chief — a dual temporal and hierarchical dimension.
G4413I.emploi: The word πρῶτος appears a considerable number of times in the New Testament. In these extracted usages, it describes people of high rank or influence in society: the chief of Galilee, the chief of a city, the chief man of an island, the chief of the Jews in Jerusalem. It can also function as an adverb to mark a logical order ("first"). All these usages refer to the idea of priority — either in time and space, or in rank and authority. The context determines the exact meaning: when it qualifies people, it almost always pertains to importance or dignity.
G4413I.portee: Understanding that "chief" describes one who has weight, authority, and influence helps grasp the dynamics of power in the biblical world. In Acts, the "chiefs" of cities or religious communities are those who can either stop the preaching of the Gospel or welcome it. Paul addresses them directly, acknowledging their position. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that the Gospel does not separate social status from God's plan: it addresses both the chief and the humble alike.

sens: That which comes first in time or space
That which occupies the highest rank, the most important
Of first order, of superior quality
The oldest or the most prior
Chief, principal
G4413J.detail:
1. That which is placed before everything else, in the order of time or space: it is that which comes first. Jesus asks the disciples to seek first the kingdom (Matthew 6:33 in implicit usages); Philippi is the first city of the district (Acts 16:12).
2. That which is of greatest importance or dignity, the most eminent in a hierarchy: the first commandment is that which takes precedence over all others (Mark 12:28-29), and the chief of the people are the leaders, the men of power (Luke 19:47).
3. That which is of fine quality, of remarkable excellence: the finest robe of the father for his restored son signifies his esteem and honor (Luke 15:22).
4. That which is older, prior in the past: expression of temporal precedence or logical priority.
5. That which is chief or principal: the first magistrates, the women of quality (Acts 17:4) designate those who have authority or high social rank.
G4413J.origine: The Greek word πρῶτος comes from a root that means "to go ahead" or "to be in front." It primarily translates in Greek the Hebrew רִאשׁוֹן (rīshôn), which also designates that which is first or principal. The word family includes terms like "before" and "priority." The basic image is that of what stands in front, which precedes, which opens the way for others.
G4413J.emploi: The word "first" is very common in the New Testament, used about 155 times. It first designates that which comes first chronologically or spatially (Acts 16:12: Philippi, the first city of the district). It also expresses rank or dignity: the first commandment of the Law (Mark 12:28-29), the first of the Jews or magistrates of the city (Acts 25:2), those who possess authority or social prestige (Acts 17:4: women of quality). The word can also qualify beauty or excellence: the finest robe (Luke 15:22). Sometimes it simply means "earlier" or "old." Its meaning thus naturally shifts from temporal or spatial sense to rank, importance, or quality.
G4413J.portee: This word reminds Christians that in the kingdom of God, priorities change: it is the first commandment — to love God with all one's heart — that orders all others. It also invites recognition of divine excellence and the beauty of restorative grace. Finally, it teaches that God calls to a new hierarchy, where the first becomes the servant of all (Matthew 20:27).

sens: One who stands in front, at the forefront
One who leads and drives others in a movement, a faction
Instigator who stirs up trouble
G4414.detail: 1. The word first evokes the image of a soldier who positions himself at the front line, ahead of all others: he is the one who leads the battle face to face. 2. Figuratively, it refers to one who takes the lead of a group, who guides and drives it — not just a simple member, but a leader. 3. In context, it specifically refers to someone who causes divisions, who stirs up controversy and trouble: in Acts 24:5, the Roman tribune accuses Paul of being the "chief" of the Nazarenes, the author of divisions among the Jews, the one whose influence divides and stirs.
G4414.origine: The word comes from "first" (πρῶτος) and the verb "to stand" (ἵστημι), literally meaning "one who stands first." It is a military image: the warrior who occupies the leading position, facing danger ahead of others. Figuratively, it naturally designates the leader, the one who gives the impetus.
G4414.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 24:5, where it qualifies Paul. Tertullus, the lawyer for the Jews, presents Paul to Governor Felix as a "chief" who stirs up divisions among all the Jews of the world and who leads the sect of the Nazarenes. The term emphasizes Paul's active role in the spread of the Christian movement and, from the perspective of his accusers, his responsibility for the troubles he causes.
G4414.portee: This word shows how Christ's adversaries perceived the apostles: not as mere believers, but as leaders capable of mobilizing the crowds and causing division. For the reader, it serves as a reminder that proclaiming the Gospel attracts opposition and can be presented as an act of rebellion. Paul accepts being the main responsible for the movement he leads.

sens: The set of privileges and advantages reserved for the firstborn son in a family
The particular status of the firstborn who became the principal heir and head of the family
What was considered a precious and inalienable possession, not to be sold or relinquished
G4415.detail:
1. The birthright refers to the special rights of the firstborn: he received a double portion of the inheritance, became the head of the family, and inherited the religious and social responsibilities of his father. It was a very honorable and highly valued status in Israel.
2. This right was so important that it could not normally be relinquished — it was a personal possession inseparable from the firstborn. When Esau sells it to Jacob for a bowl of lentils (Genesis 25:31-34), it is considered a profane and foolish act, an inexcusable lightness.
3. The biblical image emphasizes that selling or despising one's birthright is to reject what God has established and what has been given to us — a foreshadowing of the rejection of the heavenly inheritance that every Christian has received in Jesus.
G4415.origine: The word comes from "firstborn" (in Greek πρωτότοκος, from πρῶτος "first" and τόκος "birth"). Its Hebrew equivalent is בְּכוֹרָה (bekorah), which designates the rights of the בְּכוֹר (bekhor), the firstborn. All of Israel's law framed these rights: Deuteronomy 21:17 stipulates that the firstborn son receives a double portion.
G4415.emploi: This word appears only once in Hebrews 12:16, where Paul uses it to show how Esau sold his birthright for a meal — an example of profaneness and impiety. The context shows that despising this right is to reject the order established by God and to squander one's inheritance. Paul uses this example to urge Christians not to lightly abandon their own heavenly inheritance.
G4415.portee: This passage warns every believer against the lightness that would lead us to sacrifice our spiritual goods for temporal satisfactions. Esau symbolizes one who exchanges eternal inheritance for immediate pleasure. Understanding the birthright helps the Christian to measure the priceless value of his inheritance in Christ and to refuse the temptations that would seek to take it away.

sens: Child born first, in a family
One who has the birthright, the inheritance and authority
Christ, in His priority and unique superiority over creation
The resurrected Christ, first victory over death
The elect, chosen community of God
G4416.detail:
1. The firstborn is the child who is born before others, like Jesus as a child: "she gave birth to her firstborn son" (Luke 2:7). It is a simple fact of birth.

2. In Jewish law, the firstborn receives a double share of the inheritance and a particular authority in the family. The word evokes this status of privilege and power.

3. Applied to Christ, the word signifies His absolute priority over all creation: "the firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15). Not that He is created, but that everything comes from Him and is subject to Him, just as the firstborn is in his family.

4. The resurrected Christ is the "firstborn from the dead" (Colossians 1:18), the one who has conquered death first, opening the way of resurrection for others.

5. The Church, the elect, are the "congregation of the firstborn" (Hebrews 12:23): they are adopted as sons and heirs, participants in the royal status of Christ.
G4416.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "first" and "to be born." It corresponds to the Hebrew word "bekor" (בְּכוֹר), which in the Old Testament designates the firstborn son with his rights and responsibilities. In Hebrew, the word also takes on a figurative meaning: God tells the Davidic king that he will be His firstborn (Psalms 89:28), meaning clothed with royal authority. The authors of the New Testament take up this symbolic richness to express the lordship of Christ.
G4416.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament. In the Gospels, it simply describes the newborn Jesus (Luke 2:7; Matthew 1:25). But Paul and the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews imbue it with theological meaning: Christ is the firstborn of God over all creation, the one who reigns over all (Colossians 1:15), and the first resurrected one who leads a multitude of brothers into resurrection (Romans 8:29; Colossians 1:18). Revelation takes up this image: Jesus is the firstborn of the dead (Revelation 1:5). Finally, believers are collectively called "firstborn" registered in heaven (Hebrews 12:23), heirs with Christ.
G4416.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus is not a vague savior, but the concrete Lord, endowed with real authority over all creation. For the believer, it invites recognition of Christ as absolute master and to see oneself as an adopted heir, integrated into God's royal family by grace.

sens: To trip, to make a misstep
To commit a fault, a transgression
To sin, to fall short of God's command
To fail, to falter in one's conduct or faith
G4417.detail:
1. In its literal sense, stumble refers to physically tripping, making a misstep while walking. This is the primary image of the Greek word: the foot slips or catches, causing one to wobble. Although rare, this concrete meaning underlies all metaphorical uses.

2. Figuratively, to stumble means to commit a fault or a transgression. James 2:10 illustrates this: "For whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it" — the word "stumbles" translates the Greek term, as failing in just one aspect of the law is to spiritually trip.

3. To stumble in a moral context thus refers to sinning, deviating from the straight path that God lays out. A fault is a fall of the soul, akin to an unsteady step. In James 3:2, "we all stumble in many ways" reminds us that everyone morally trips, particularly through speech.

4. Finally, to stumble can mean to fail, to falter in one's conduct or perseverance. In 2 Peter 1:10, the apostle encourages believers to "never stumble," meaning to stand firm in their calling and not to falter.
G4417.origine: The Greek verb πταίω comes from a root that evokes the movement of the foot, the act of stumbling or slipping. In Hebrew, it often translates נָגַף (nagaph), which means to strike, to cause to fall, to reach with a blow. The basic idea is that of a fall or a misstep, initially physical, then transposed to the moral and spiritual realm. The word family shares this image of wavering or instability.
G4417.emploi: The verb πταίω appears four times in the New Testament, always in the epistles. Romans 11:11 uses it to describe the stumbling of Israel: did they "stumble" so as to fall beyond recovery? No — their misstep paradoxically opened salvation to the Gentiles. James uses it twice: in 2:10, to show that a single transgression renders one guilty (even one who keeps the whole law "stumbles" if he violates one), and in 3:2, where the apostle states that "we all stumble" in words as well as deeds — no one escapes fault. In 2 Peter 1:10, the exhortation reverses the meaning: "you will never stumble" means that the strengthening of one's calling guarantees perseverance. In all cases, the word carries the idea of a failure, minor or grave, of the believer.
G4417.portee: This word reminds us of two essential truths. First, that the Christian is not exempt from faults: "we all stumble" (James 3:2) invites humility and compassion towards brothers. Second, that even apparent sin (the stumbling of Israel) can fit into God's plan, from which good emerges (Romans 11:11). Finally, the call to not stumble (2 Peter 1:10) encourages vigilance and strengthening in faith, knowing that stability comes from the assurance of one's election in Christ.

sens: The back part of the foot, below the ankle
One who treads or tramples on someone (figuratively)
An attitude of contempt or betrayal towards one whom one pretended to serve
G4418.detail:
1. The heel is the fleshy and bony part that forms the back of the foot, beneath the ankle. It is the natural point of support when walking or standing. In John 13:18, Jesus quotes Psalm 41:10 when speaking of the one "who eats bread with me," in other words, who shares his meal: this man "has lifted his heel against me," meaning he has trampled or crushed Jesus' trust as one would crush something with the heel.
2. The image of the lifted heel evokes a triumphant or aggressive step on someone else: it is one who, until then a friend or companion, turns and tramples underfoot the one he seemed to support or honor.
3. Thus, it is an act of betrayal and contempt: not a sudden and violent attack, but a demonstration of rejection towards someone close, to whom loyalty was owed.
G4418.origine: The Greek word *pterna* (heel) corresponds to the Hebrew *aqeb* from the Old Testament. This same image of the lifted heel against someone appears in Psalm 41:10 (Hebrew), which describes the betrayal of a friend: "Even my close friend, someone I trusted, who shared my bread, has turned against me." Both terms, Hebrew and Greek, belong to the simple physical vocabulary of the human body.
G4418.emploi: The word *pterna* appears only once in the New Testament, in John 13:18. Jesus uses it to interpret Judas' betrayal by linking it to a prophecy from the Old Testament. In doing so, he transforms a simple physical image (the heel of the foot) into a symbol of rejection and disloyalty. The expression "to lift one's heel against someone" is not literal: it means to turn against someone, to despise, to betray despite the appearance of friendship.
G4418.portee: This word from Jesus shows us how the most painful betrayal comes from one with whom we have shared the intimacy of a meal. It also warns us that Jesus knew in advance Judas' reaction and that, even in the face of disloyalty, he remained in control of the situation. For the believer, it is a lesson in humility: to recognize that even among close ones, trust can be wounded, and that only God truly sees and judges the heart.

sens: Small wing or projection
Summit, elevated point of a building
Pinnacle or wing of the temple
G4419.detail: 1. The word comes from a root meaning "wing"; it is a diminutive that designates a small wing or a shape resembling a wing. 2. By extension, it refers to an architectural projection of a building: a cornice, a part that protrudes, a summit. 3. In the Gospel, it specifically applies to the "top of the temple" — probably a high point, a wing or a projection of the Jerusalem sanctuary from which the view of the city was dizzying. Matthew 4:5 and Luke 4:9 recount that the devil placed Jesus there to tempt him: "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here" (Luke 4:9). The place is high enough that the jump would be fatal.
G4419.origine: The word comes from the Greek πτέρυξ (ptéryx), which means "wing," and carries the diminutive form -ιον, which creates a sense of "small wing" or "thing shaped like a wing." In Hebrew, the word כָּנָף (kanaf) is often found, which also means "wing," and is also used figuratively to designate the extremities or projections of a construction. The Greek diminutive gives the idea of something fine, light, that protrudes or rises.
G4419.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, always to designate the "top of the temple" in Jerusalem. Matthew 4:5 reports the second temptation of Jesus in the desert: the devil transports him to the holy city and places him on the top of the temple. Luke 4:9 provides a parallel account and adds the challenge: "throw yourself down from here." In both cases, the context is one of temptation: the devil urges Jesus to jump from a high point of the temple to test his trust in God and his divine sonship. The use of the word emphasizes the extreme height and danger of the location.
G4419.portee: This word illustrates a trick of the devil: he does not always attack with brute force, but by twisting God's promises and pushing towards acts of presumption. The temptation on the top of the temple shows that even knowledge of Scriptures (the devil quotes Psalm 91) can be perverted to serve doubt and pride. For the believer, it is a reminder that true faith is not a spectacular demonstration, but a quiet trust in God, even when everything seems lost.

sens: Organ that allows birds and creatures to fly
Maternal or divine protection that shelters and gathers
Attribute of celestial beings seen in vision
G4420.detail:
1. The wing is the organ of the bird's body that allows it to fly. This is the primary and physical meaning of the word (Revelation 4:8, 9:9, 12:14).
2. Figuratively, the wing evokes protection, shelter, and the tenderness of a mother gathering her young. Jesus uses this image to express his desire to protect Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings (Matthew 23:37, Luke 13:34): it is the image of one who wishes to keep safe from danger.
3. In the visions of Revelation, wings characterize celestial beings (angelic creatures, the eagle): they mark their superhuman nature and their ability to move in the divine realm, to fulfill God's will (Revelation 4:8, 12:14).
G4420.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "peto" which means "to fly." It corresponds to the Hebrew "kanaf" (כנף) in the Old Testament, which refers to both the physical wing and divine protection, shelter. In both Hebrew and Greek, the word carries the idea of movement and safety.
G4420.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in the sense of wing. Two instances concern the literal wings of celestial beings seen in vision (Revelation 4:8 and 9:9): the four living creatures and the locusts of the fifth trumpet. Two other instances (Matthew 23:37, Luke 13:34) use the wing as an image of divine maternal protection: Jesus wishes to gather the children of Jerusalem under his wings, but they refuse. A final instance (Revelation 12:14) describes the wings of the eagle that carry the woman into the wilderness to escape the serpent.
G4420.portee: This word invites the reader to see the protective love of the Lord: the wings evoke a safe refuge, a tenderness that shelters. When Jesus expresses his desire to gather Jerusalem under his wings, he reveals his shepherd's heart. For today's Christian, it is a promise that divine protection is never far away for those who accept it.

sens: flying animal with feathers and wings
living creature distinct from humans, quadrupeds, and fish
G4421.detail:
1. The word literally designates the animal that flies thanks to its wings and feathers — it is the bird in the ordinary sense. It is a descriptive term that emphasizes the ability to fly (the word comes from a root meaning "to fly").
2. In its biblical usage, "bird" mainly serves to classify living creatures: in 1 Corinthians 15:39, Paul enumerates the different kinds of flesh — that of humans, that of four-legged beasts, that of birds, that of fish — to show that creation takes on very varied forms. This is an argument for the diversity of life created by God.
G4421.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to fly" or "to be able to fly." It is an adjective ("winged," "flying") that becomes a noun when used alone to mean "the winged one" or "the one that flies" — that is, the bird. The formation of the word highlights what characterizes the bird: its ability to fly.
G4421.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 15:39. Paul uses it to enumerate the different categories of living creatures and to show that flesh varies considerably depending on whether it belongs to a human, a quadruped, a bird, or a fish. This passage prepares the argument that the resurrection of the dead, although mysterious, is no more absurd than this natural diversity that we observe every day.
G4421.portee: This word invites the Christian to contemplate the variety and richness of divine creation. The mention of birds alongside other creatures reminds us that God did not create a uniform and monotonous world, but a universe of infinite richness. This reinforces the idea that the Creator is capable of realizing the resurrection of the body, having already shown his creative power in this wonderful diversity.

sens: To experience a sudden and intense fear
To be seized by a fear that paralyzes
To be troubled by an alarming appearance or news
G4422.detail:
1. The word expresses a fear that suddenly grips, a terror that invades the soul. In Luke 21:9, Jesus tells his disciples not to be frightened when they hear of wars and uprisings: this is not a fleeting worry, but that panic which could paralyze them.
2. It is a fear that disturbs and unsettles, often in the face of the unexpected or the strange. In Luke 24:37, the resurrected disciples are seized with fear upon seeing the resurrected Jesus: their fear is so intense that they first take him for a spirit.
3. The word also describes the state of one who is deeply troubled, as if shaken by a sudden fear that takes away all assurance. It is that terror that freezes one in place.
G4422.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes trembling and fright. The Greek Old Testament used this term to translate the Hebrew חָתַת (hathat), which literally means to be broken or shattered by fear, to be torn apart internally by terror. This image of internal rupture explains why the word carries the idea of a fear that deeply destabilizes.
G4422.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Gospel of Luke, always in the passive form ("to be frightened"). First in Luke 21:9, where Jesus exhorts his disciples not to be dominated by fear in the face of wars and troubles to come. Then in Luke 24:37, where the resurrected disciples, seeing the resurrected Christ, are seized with panic, thinking they see a ghost. In both cases, the context shows a fear that could block faith or understanding: Jesus invites them not to be enslaved by it, and the disciples must overcome this fear to recognize the Lord.
G4422.portee: This word reminds us that fear is a reality in the life of the disciple, but that Jesus calls us not to be dominated by it. The fear of the future, alarming news, the unexpected — all these elements can terrify us; but Christ invites us to a trust that transcends fear. It is also an invitation to be taught by the Lord rather than to be paralyzed by panic: the disciples had to overcome their terror to recognize the resurrected Jesus.

sens: State of agitation or disturbance of the mind caused by fear
Fear that shakes the soul and disturbs it
G4423.detail:
1. "To disturb" literally designates an agitation, an emotional shake provoked mainly by fear. It is the disordered inner state of one who is afraid: their heart races, their mind is troubled. In 1 Peter 3:6, the text exhorts believing women to "not be disturbed by any fear," meaning not to be shaken or perturbed by fear.
2. The word evokes an emotion that jolts, that stirs: it is not a simple awareness of danger, but an inner reaction that disrupts the peace of the one who experiences it. That is why the translation speaks of being "disturbed" — the disturbance comes from fear; it is its natural consequence on the heart and mind.
G4423.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "ptoeo" (πτοέω), which means "to be frightened" or "to be afraid." The root evokes the idea of a shake, a sudden agitation. The Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew "pachad" (פַּחַד), which means "fear" or "dread" with this word. It is a word that paints the emotion in action: not fear as thought, but as turbulence of the heart.
G4423.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:6. Peter uses it to encourage women to live in purity and righteousness without allowing fear — that of the world, of judgment, of mockery — to agitate or divert them from virtue. The context shows that "to disturb" opposes the firmness of one who remains attached to God despite external pressures. It is the disturbance of the soul caused by fear when one is not grounded in faith.
G4423.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize how fear agitates and troubles the soul. For the Christian, it is a call not to be shaken by the fear of the world, but to maintain the balance and serenity that trust in God provides. It is a reminder that faith calms this inner disturbance, while fear provokes it.

sens: Port city of Phoenicia, on the Mediterranean coast of the Levant.
G4424.detail: Ptolemais is a coastal city located in Phoenicia (the ancient region corresponding to present-day Lebanon). It is an important port on the Mediterranean, where the Apostle Paul and his companions stop during their journey to Jerusalem as reported in Acts 21:7.
G4424.origine: The name Ptolemais comes from Greek and honors the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt, which dominated this region during the Hellenistic period. The city was formerly called Akko in Hebrew and retained that name before being renamed. It kept the name Ptolemais during the New Testament period.
G4424.emploi: Ptolemais appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:7, during Paul's return journey from his third missionary trip. Paul arrives there by ship from Tyre and stops to greet and spend a day with the Christian disciples of the city, illustrating the connections between the young churches of the Mediterranean basin.

sens: Flat instrument used to separate grain from chaff
Symbol of divine judgment that separates the righteous from the wicked
G4425.detail:
1. The winnowing fork is a simple agricultural tool: a flat tray or wide shovel, often made of wood, that the farmer fills with threshed grain mixed with chaff. He throws it into the air so that the wind carries away the light chaff while the heavier grain falls back down. This results in pure grain, ready to be stored or ground. John the Baptist speaks of the "winnowing fork" that the Messiah holds in his hand (Matthew 3:12, Luke 3:17): a concrete image of agricultural work that every Jew was well acquainted with.
2. This agricultural image becomes a powerful figure of judgment: just as the winnowing fork separates useful grain from useless chaff, Jesus will separate the elect (the grain, kept in the barn) from those who will be judged (the chaff, burned in the fire). Thus, it is a symbol of a definitive and inevitable decision.
G4425.origine: The Greek word πτύον comes from a root indicating the action of winnowing, sifting by the wind. In Hebrew, the same action was expressed by words related to agriculture: הנפה (hanafah, "to winnow") or דברי (dabar, "grain"). The winnowing fork is not a sophisticated tool but a popular one, well known in the Eastern Mediterranean. Its use dates back to antiquity: every grain farmer used it after threshing.
G4425.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the discourse of John the Baptist in Matthew (3:12) and Luke (3:17). The two texts are identical: John describes Jesus coming with his winnowing fork in hand to judge the world. The image is simple but loaded with spiritual significance: it announces a practical and complete judgment. There is no nuance between the two uses: it is always the instrument of the final sorting. Why this word rather than another? Because it reinforces the idea that judgment is just and necessary, just as winnowing grain is.
G4425.portee: This image of the winnowing fork invites the believer to reflect on the reality of divine judgment: it is not an abstract threat, but a concrete separation between what pleases God and what does not. For the reader of the Gospels, it calls to question: am I the grain or the chaff? Will I be kept or rejected? This simple yet striking image makes the coming judgment feel less distant and more personal.

sens: To be seized with fear, terror in the face of something frightening
To be intimidated or troubled by a threat
To lose confidence or become paralyzed by fear
G4426.detail:
1. The word describes the state of one who is suddenly seized with fear in the face of danger or a threat. It is a fear that grips, that deeply troubles. In Philippians 1:28, Paul warns Christians: they should not be frightened by the opponents who oppose their faith.
2. More broadly, it means to be intimidated or troubled to the point of losing one's assurance. One who is frightened wavers, hesitates, and may even retreat in the face of opposition or persecution.
3. It also extends to being morally troubled or shaken, losing confidence and courage in the face of an external threat.
G4426.origine: The word comes from a Greek root related to the idea of trembling or being agitated. It expresses this involuntary movement of the body and soul when fear seizes us. The form used here is the middle or passive (ptúromai), which means that it is something that happens to the person, that seizes them, rather than something they do.
G4426.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 1:28. Paul uses it to exhort the church in Philippi not to be frightened by those who persecute them. In this context, fear in the face of opponents would be a bad sign, as it would show a weakness of faith. On the contrary, standing firm without fear is for the Christian the proof that their salvation is assured, while for the persecutors it is a sign of their condemnation.
G4426.portee: This word invites the Christian not to yield to fear in the face of the opposition and threats that the world directs at their faith. Paul teaches us that fear of our enemies weakens us spiritually and can divert us from Christ, while firm trust in God is the visible sign of our belonging to salvation. It is a call to boldness and unwavering faith.

sens: Liquid secreted by the salivary glands in the mouth
Symbol of defilement or dishonor in biblical cultures
Instrument used by Jesus to heal
G4427.detail:
1. Saliva is the natural liquid secreted by the glands in our mouth to aid in digestion and speech. It is a very concrete reality of the human body. In John 9:6, Jesus spits on the ground and mixes his saliva with the mud to form a paste that he applies to the eyes of the blind man.

2. In ancient Near Eastern cultures, spitting on someone was an act of insult and contempt, a mark of rejection. Conversely, in some contexts, saliva was attributed with healing or blessing virtues, particularly those of kings or holy men.

3. The passage in John 9:6 reveals that Jesus does not hesitate to use sensitive and material gestures to accomplish his miracles: he does not heal merely by word, but by touching people and using concrete elements like water and mud. This humble gesture reinforces the mystery of the incarnation — God acts through a true body.
G4427.origine: The Greek word πτύσμα comes from the verb πτύω (ptúô), which means "to spit." The word literally designates what is spat: saliva. The family of the word also includes the noun πτύσις (the act of spitting) and the adjective πτύαρος. The act of spitting appears in several places in the Gospel, notably to express contempt or, here, as an act of healing.
G4427.emploi: The word πτύσμα appears only once in the New Testament, in John 9:6, during the healing of the blind man. It is a specific word, uncommon even in classical Greek. Its unique use in this narrative is very significant: Jesus uses his own saliva mixed with mud to form a remedy that will restore sight to the blind man. This gesture combines the material humility of the human body with the power of Jesus' word and act, emphasizing that the miracle does not depend on a magical formula, but on the very person of Jesus and his compassion for the suffering.
G4427.portee: This account teaches us that Jesus is not too exalted or too pure to enter into our concrete and physical misery. He heals by touching, believing, and humbling himself. For the reader, it reminds us that the risen Christ does not disdain our sick bodies, our earthly limitations: he honors and transforms them. It is an encouragement to pray for the healing of the sick, knowing that God cares for us even in our flesh.

sens: To wrap, fold over on itself a flexible object like a scroll or a book
To close, fold to store or conclude
G4428.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of rolling or wrapping something flexible. In its only occurrence in the New Testament, it refers to closing a written scroll: Jesus, after reading from the prophet Isaiah in the synagogue, "rolls" the book and hands it back to the attendant (Luke 4:20). It is the gesture of one who finishes reading and puts the object away.
2. Figuratively, the verb means to close, conclude, or bring something to an end. The image of rolling suggests a movement that gathers and stores, putting a final point.
G4428.origine: The verb comes from a root that evokes the movement of folding and rolling. In Greek, the prefix ἀνα- (ἀνα-πτύσσω) means "to unroll," which shows that πτύσσω denotes the opposite action: to fold or roll. This word is specifically used for objects that can be rolled — scrolls of papyrus or parchment, books of antiquity — making it a technical term in the world of writings.
G4428.emploi: The verb πτύσσω appears only once in the New Testament. Jesus, having read the prophecy of Isaiah in the synagogue of Nazareth, "rolls" the book — that is, he closes it by wrapping it — and hands it to the synagogue attendant. This simple and concrete gesture, that of concluding an official reading, marks the transition from the moment when Jesus teaches to when he sits among the astonished assembly. The action of rolling the book emphasizes that the public reading is finished and that Jesus is about to assert that this prophetic text has been fulfilled in his presence.
G4428.portee: This word reminds us of a detail in the narrative that shows Jesus within the framework of Jewish customs: he honors the Torah, he respects the practices of the synagogue. But by rolling the book and sitting down, he is about to make a radical statement about himself, which shows that obedience to the Law and the revelation of his mission are not opposed. For the reader, this concrete gesture humanizes Jesus and prepares for the turning point of the narrative.

sens: To project saliva from the mouth
To use saliva as a means of healing or action
G4429.detail:
1. To spit means to reject saliva from the mouth, a very physical and direct gesture. This is what Jesus does in John 9:6 when he spits on the ground to make mud that he will apply to the eyes of the blind man.
2. In Mark, the word refers more to the saliva itself used for healing: in Mark 7:33 and 8:23, Jesus puts his saliva on the tongue of the deaf-mute and on the eyes of the blind man. It is a gesture of healing, where saliva becomes an instrument of Jesus' power. In Jewish and Mediterranean culture, saliva was reputed to have healing properties.
G4429.origine: The Greek word πτύω comes from a root that imitates the sound and act of spitting (onomatopoeia). It appears in other Greek forms such as ἐκπτύω (to spit out) and ἐμπτύω (to spit against someone). The Greek Old Testament uses this word to translate the Hebrew יָרָק (yaraq) in Numbers 12:14, where spitting on someone is an act of insult and contempt.
G4429.emploi: The verb πτύω appears three times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels and all related to healing miracles. Mark uses it twice: in Mark 7:33 for the account of the deaf-mute, where Jesus spits or puts his saliva to heal; in Mark 8:23 for the blind man of Bethsaida. John 9:6 reports the same type of action with the man born blind. The biblical usage completely transforms the meaning: spitting, a gesture of insult or disgust in pagan culture, becomes for Jesus a sign of his compassion and power over infirmities. Saliva is the visible medium of his invisible power.
G4429.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus does not hesitate to perform simple, human, concrete gestures to heal. He does not rely solely on words; he touches, he spits, he lowers himself to the level of those who suffer. It is an encouragement for the believer: God draws near to us in our misery, not by remaining distant or contemptuous, but by making himself vulnerable and entering into our condition to set us free.

sens: Body of a deceased person
Dead body abandoned without burial
Image of destruction or ruin
G4430.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the body of a deceased person, particularly after a violent or tragic death. Matthew 14:12 recounts how "the disciples of John came and took his body" after the execution of John the Baptist: it refers to the corpse that must be buried. It is a respectful term that acknowledges the dignity of what remains of the deceased.
2. The word sometimes emphasizes the tragic aspect of an abandoned corpse, without funeral honor. In Revelation 11:9, the corpses of the two witnesses lie "in the street of the great city" without being buried: the image expresses humiliation and contempt. Matthew 24:28 uses the proverbial image of the corpse attracting eagles to evoke a place of inevitable calamity.
3. By extension, the word can signify destruction or ruin, which anchors it in its Greek etymology (a "fall").
G4430.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to fall." It literally designates what has fallen — first a building in ruins, then by extension the body of a fallen creature, that is, dead. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses different words depending on the context (פֶּרֶץ for a breach, מַפֶּלֶת for a fall), showing that each language emphasizes a different aspect of dying: the fall, destruction, collapse.
G4430.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, primarily in Matthew, Mark, and Revelation. It is always used for a true dead body, never in a figurative sense. Matthew and Mark use it for the corpse of John the Baptist (Matthew 14:12 and Mark 6:29) and for that of Jesus entrusted to Joseph of Arimathea (Mark 15:45). Revelation uses it for the two witnesses dead in Jerusalem (11:8-9), emphasizing the indignity of leaving their corpses unburied. In each case, the word underscores the material and often painful aspect of death: a body that must be treated with respect or that suffers outrage.
G4430.portee: This word reminds the believer of the physical reality of death and the importance of treating the dead with dignity. The accounts show that even after the crucifixion, the care given to the body of Jesus (Mark 15:45) expresses honor and love. The image of the corpse in Revelation warns that the refusal of burial is an extreme form of humiliation, but also that God watches over his own even in death. The word thus restores a healthy biblical view of our physical nature.

sens: The collapse of a structure, the physical destruction of a building
The catastrophic event, the action of falling or collapsing
Figuratively, the moral or spiritual downfall of a person, their inner collapse
G4431.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the complete collapse of a house or structure. In Matthew 7:27, Jesus describes the house built on sand that collapses under rain and wind: its "ruin" (πτῶσις) is great, which shows the extent of the destruction.

2. The word can also emphasize the event itself, the moment when something falls or collapses, rather than the ruined state that results from it.

3. Figuratively, Luke 2:34 speaks of the "fall" of many in Israel caused by Jesus: this is not a physical ruin, but the spiritual collapse of those who reject him, their moral and religious downfall.
G4431.origine: The Greek word πτῶσις comes from the verb πίπτω ("to fall"), whose root evokes the movement of descent. The family of this verb also includes words for "fall," "one who falls," or "that which has fallen." In Hebrew, the underlying word in the Greek Old Testament is often נֶגֶף ("blow, plague") or מַפֶּלֶת ("ruin, debris"), which share the idea of destruction or brutal collapse.
G4431.emploi: The word πτῶσις appears only twice in the New Testament. In Matthew 7:27, Jesus uses it to speak of the material destruction of a poorly founded house: this is its proper and concrete meaning. In Luke 2:34, Simeon uses it figuratively to announce that Jesus will cause the spiritual downfall of some in Israel (those who reject him) and the exaltation of others (those who believe). The context shows that this word is never neutral: it denotes real destruction, whether physical or moral, never just a simple difficulty.
G4431.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that foundations matter. In Matthew 7:27, Jesus shows that building one's life on anything other than his word leads to ruin. In Luke 2:34, the image of spiritual downfall warns that rejecting Jesus leads to inner collapse, while acceptance brings restoration. These two passages invite the believer to examine their own foundations.

sens: State of material lack, extreme deprivation
Precarious financial situation, absence of resources
Inner state of detachment or spiritual humility
G4432.detail:
1. Poverty primarily refers to the most complete material deprivation: not having what is necessary. It is the Greek word for "begging" or "extreme indigence." In Revelation 2:9, the church in Smyrna experiences poverty, meaning it suffers from real material deprivation.

2. It can also describe a situation of economic lack that one is going through, without necessarily being at the threshold of begging. In 2 Corinthians 8:2, Paul speaks of the deep poverty of the churches in Macedonia, victims of tribulations and trials: this is their difficult living condition.

3. When Christ becomes poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), Paul refers to more than just a simple decrease in income: he speaks of a lowering, a humiliation, a voluntary detachment from wealth. The poverty of Christ becomes the image of his renunciation and love.
G4432.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb πτωχεύω (ptōcheuō), which means "to be poor" or "to beg." The root evokes the image of one who bends down, who lowers themselves — the poor is one who bows their head, who asks for alms. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word primarily translates the Hebrew עֳנִי (onyī), which denotes affliction and material distress. The entire family of this word carries the idea of lowering and insufficiency.
G4432.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the context of church life or the mystery of Christ. In 2 Corinthians 8:2 and 8:9, Paul uses it to speak of a paradoxical transformation: despite poverty (tribulations, lack), joy abounds, and through the poverty of Christ comes our spiritual enrichment. In Revelation 2:9, Jesus acknowledges the real material poverty of his church, but reveals to her that she is rich in him. The word always carries a nuance of trial or spiritual mystery.
G4432.portee: This word reminds Christians that material poverty is not shameful, but invites one to seek true riches in Christ. The example of the Macedonians and the sacrifice of Christ teach that joy and generosity arise not from earthly abundance, but from love and faith. For the believer who is poor or in distress, these verses are a promise: your poverty can become a path of grace.

sens: to beg, to live as a beggar
to be in need, to lack the essentials
to voluntarily reduce oneself to poverty
G4433.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to one who begs, who lives by asking for alms — this is the most concrete image of the poor in distress.
2. More broadly, it means to be poor, to lack essential resources, to be in need: it is the opposite of being rich and comfortable.
3. In particular, Paul uses this verb in 2 Corinthians 8:9 to describe how Christ voluntarily lowered himself to poverty: "who for your sake became poor, though he was rich." This is a poverty chosen out of love, the Son of God accepting total deprivation.
G4433.origine: The word comes from the adjective πτωχός (poor), which evokes the image of a man bent down, burdened, reduced to little. The root is ancient in Greek: it suggests the idea of bending down, of lowering oneself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word translated the Hebrew דָּלַל (to be weak, impoverished), יָרַשׁ (to possess little, to inherit little), and רוּשׁ (to be destitute). It is a word that describes less a static state than a process: to become poor, to fall into need.
G4433.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 8:9. Paul uses it to celebrate the incarnation of Christ: the Lord, infinitely rich in his heavenly glory, voluntarily became poor by coming to earth, accepting the precarious human condition, so that we might be spiritually enriched by his grace. This is a decisive moment in the Gospel: God descends into deprivation to lift us up.
G4433.portee: This word shows us that Jesus did not remain in comfort: he chose poverty, lack, humility, to join us and save us.
